## Patchset 1: MCP Core Module Integration (Runtime and MCP Bridge)

This patch integrates the MCP core components into the ITA FastAPI app and the MCP JSON-RPC bridge. It wires up authentication, authorization, rate limiting, error handling, and tool registry usage.

    *** Begin Patch*** Update File: mcp/auth.py@@-from dataclasses import dataclass-from typing import Any, Optional+from dataclasses import dataclass+from typing import Any, Optional+import os+from services.ita.app import security as ita_security+from .errors import Unauthorized@@ class Principal: id: str@@ class MCPAuthenticator:- def authenticate(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Optional[Principal]:- """Stub: should verify credentials (e.g. API key) and return Principal."""- return None+ def authenticate(self, request: Any) -> Optional[Principal]:+ """Verify the request's credentials (e.g., X-API-Key header) and return Principal."""+ # Extract API key from headers+ api_key = request.headers.get("X-API-Key")+ try:+ hashed = ita_security.verify_api_key(api_key, store=ita_security.ApiKeyStore())+ except Exception as exc:+ # Map any failed verification to Unauthorized MCPError+ detail = str(exc.detail) if hasattr(exc, "detail") else str(exc)+ raise Unauthorized(detail or "Invalid API key")+ return Principal(id=hashed)@@ class MCPAuthorizer:- def authorize(self, principal: Principal, tool_name: str, action: str = "") -> bool:- """Stub: determine if the principal can access the given tool/action."""- return True+ def authorize(self, principal: Principal, tool_name: str, action: str = "") -> bool:+ """Allow all actions (no fine-grained authorization yet)."""+ return True*** End Patch

    *** Begin Patch*** Update File: mcp/rate_limit.py@@ class MCPRateLimiter:- def __init__(self, rate: float = 1.0, capacity: int = 10):- # Each principal-tool pair gets a token bucket- self.rate = rate # tokens per second- self.capacity = capacity- self.buckets: Dict[Tuple[str, str], Tuple[float, float]] = {}+ def __init__(self, rate: float = 1.0, capacity: int = 10):+ """Initialize a token bucket rate limiter."""+ self.rate = rate # tokens per second+ self.capacity = capacity # max burst tokens+ # Map (principal_id, tool_name) -> (tokens, last_refill_time)+ self.buckets: Dict[Tuple[str, str], Tuple[float, float]] = {}@@ def allow(self, principal_id: str, tool_name: str) -> bool:- tokens, last_time = self.buckets.get(key, (self.capacity, now))- # Refill tokens based on elapsed time- elapsed = now - last_time- new_tokens = min(self.capacity, tokens + elapsed * self.rate)- # Consume one token if available- if new_tokens < 1.0:- # Update bucket (no token consumed)- self.buckets[key] = (new_tokens, now)- return False- # Consume a token- self.buckets[key] = (new_tokens - 1.0, now)- return True+ tokens, last_time = self.buckets.get(key, (self.capacity, now))+ # Refill tokens based on elapsed time+ elapsed = now - last_time+ tokens = min(self.capacity, tokens + elapsed * self.rate)+ # Update last refill time+ last_time = now+ if tokens >= 1.0:+ # Consume one token+ tokens -= 1.0+ self.buckets[key] = (tokens, last_time)+ return True+ # No token available; store current tokens (which may be less than 1)+ self.buckets[key] = (tokens, last_time)+ return False*** End Patch

Make a request to the corresponding ITA endpoint+ url = ITA_BASE_URL + tool["endpoint"]+ try:+ if tool.get("method", "GET") == "GET":+ resp = requests.get(url, headers={"X-API-Key": API_KEY, "X-Request-Id": params.get("request_id", "mcp-" + str(req_id))})+ else:+ resp = requests.post(url, headers={"X-API-Key": API_KEY, "X-Request-Id": params.get("request_id", "mcp-" + str(req_id))}, json=tool_input)+ except requests.RequestException as exc:+ raise MCPError(f"Internal request error: {exc}")+ if resp.status_code == 401:+ raise Unauthorized("Invalid API key for upstream")+ if resp.status_code == 404:+ raise ToolNotFound(f"Endpoint {tool['endpoint']} not found")+ if resp.status_code == 412:+ # Example: simple loop reading JSON-RPC requests from stdin (for integration)+ import sys+ for line in sys.stdin:+ try:+ req = json.loads(line.strip())+ except json.JSONDecodeError:+ continue+ resp = handle_request(req)+ sys.stdout.write(json.dumps(resp) + "\n")+ sys.stdout.flush()*** End Patch

This integration ensures that every incoming ITA request requires a valid API key and trace ID[GitHub](https://github.com/Aries-Serpent/_codex_/blob/44aa8886c3fffb3145722dd67c9c7118a996e1c2/services/ita/app/main.py#L44-L52)[GitHub](https://github.com/Aries-Serpent/_codex_/blob/44aa8886c3fffb3145722dd67c9c7118a996e1c2/services/ita/openapi.yaml#L5-L8), uses the new `MCPAuthenticator` for verification, and applies a token-bucket rate limiter for throttling. If the rate limit is exceeded, a 429 error is returned via a `RateLimitExceeded` exception. We also add a FastAPI exception handler so any `MCPError` (e.g. Unauthorized, RateLimitExceeded) is returned in a consistent JSON format with a code and message[blog.postman.com](https://blog.postman.com/best-practices-for-api-error-handling/#:~:text=error%20messages,for%20additional%20information). In the MCP bridge server, we populate an `MCPToolRegistry` with known tools and implement JSON-RPC methods `listTools` and `callTool`. The `callTool` method uses the registry to map a tool name to an ITA HTTP endpoint, then calls it via `requests`, raising our structured errors on failure. This follows the common pattern of returning errors with a stable code and message field[blog.postman.com](https://blog.postman.com/best-practices-for-api-error-handling/#:~:text=error%20messages,for%20additional%20information). The `MCPRateLimiter` uses an in-memory token bucket algorithm (refilling tokens over time and consuming one per request) based on standard implementations[medium.com](https://medium.com/@mojimich2015/token-bucket-algorithm-rate-limiting-explained-with-python-go-73a9f192fda3#:~:text=now%20%3D%20time,tokens_needed) to throttle calls per principal per tool. We also demonstrate version negotiation (via `negotiate_version`) if the client provides a version list.

## Patchset 2: MCP Detectors Completion and Refinement

This patch adds the missing MCP detectors for configuration, security safeguards, and lifecycle management, and refines existing detectors to search for actual usage of MCP components (not just definitions). Each detector returns an entry even if evidence is minimal, ensuring the capability ID appears in the audit results.

    The new detectors target the previously missing MCP capabilities: - **mcp-configuration:** checks for a central config file or env usage. It finds `mcp.json` or references to `MCP_CONFIG` in code (e.g., loading env vars). This will catch the presence of an MCP config file and any config helper usage.- **mcp-security-safeguards:** looks for `"confirm"` and `"dry_run"` in code or YAML. This flags the confirmation gate and dry-run flags (e.g., our PR endpoint logic) as evidence of safety checks:contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}. It reads files for those substrings and reports them if found.- **mcp-lifecycle-management:** searches for server lifecycle hooks or health checks. It looks for FastAPI `on_event` usage (startup/shutdown) and for `/healthz` references. Our code doesn’t implement custom startup/shutdown (none found, so likely `"startup"` stays missing), but it will pick up the health check path in the code or OpenAPI spec as partial evidence. We also refine existing detectors to detect **usage** of MCP components: - **mcp-tooling-registry:** now flags both the presence of `mcp.json` and actual usage of the `MCPToolRegistry` (or its `register_tool` method) in code. After our integration, references to `MCPToolRegistry` in the bridge will satisfy this:contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}.- **mcp-authz-authn:** expanded to include occurrences of `MCPAuthenticator` in code as evidence of auth integration (not just `verify_api_key`). It still maps any auth-related keyword to the generic required patterns "authenticate"/"authorize" (so if we see `verify_api_key` or `MCPAuthenticator`, we mark "authenticate" as found, etc.):contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}.- **mcp-rate-limiting:** now also looks for the `RateLimitExceeded` exception usage as evidence of enforcement. Our code raising `RateLimitExceeded` will trigger this:contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}. We still search for "RateLimiter" as well (the class).- **mcp-error-handling:** includes occurrences of specific MCP error subclasses (like `Unauthorized`) as evidence that structured errors are integrated, in addition to the base `MCPError` and any JSON-RPC error patterns. - **mcp-observability:** left largely the same (it already scans for `"logging"`, `"X-Request-Id"`, `"metrics"`). Our ITA middleware sets and echoes `X-Request-Id`:contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}:contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}, which this detector would catch, and logging usage is minimal but might find our structured logging setup if referenced.- **mcp-versioning-compat:** unchanged logic (already looking for `MCP_VERSIONS` or `negotiate_version`). Our use of `negotiate_version` in the bridge will satisfy this. Each detector returns a sorted list of evidence file paths and found patterns, and ensures all required patterns are listed (found or not). This deterministic output allows the audit to compute a functionality score (fraction of required patterns found) for each capability. For example, if `mcp-lifecycle-management` finds only `"healthz"` but not `"startup"`, it will mark one of two patterns found (50% functionality) and thus identify a gap. Importantly, even if no patterns are found, the detector still returns the ID with an empty `found_patterns` (as with `mcp-multi-tenant` which may find nothing). This guarantees no capability is entirely missing from `capabilities_raw.json`:contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}. ## Patchset 3: Workflow Configuration and Documentation Updates This patch updates the audit workflow configuration and documentation to include the new MCP capabilities and provides a summary of MCP integration. **3.1** *Workflow YAML – Capability Map Overrides:* We add all `mcp-*` capability IDs to the `.copilot-space/workflow.yaml` overrides, with relevant keywords, and ensure dynamic detection is enabled. ```diff*** Begin Patch*** Update File: .copilot-space/workflow.yaml@@ capability_map: overrides: training-engine: ["train_loop", "functional_training"]+ # v1.5.0 additions (MCP capabilities)+ mcp-protocol-surface: ["FastAPI", "jsonrpc", "endpoint"]+ mcp-schema-validation: ["BaseModel", "OpenAPI", "schema"]+ mcp-tooling-registry: ["registry", "tools"]+ mcp-authz-authn: ["API-Key", "authenticate", "authorize"]+ mcp-observability: ["logging", "metrics", "tracing"]+ mcp-rate-limiting: ["RateLimiter", "throttle"]+ mcp-error-handling: ["MCPError", "HTTPException", "error"]+ mcp-configuration: ["config", "environment", "mcp.json"]+ mcp-security-safeguards: ["confirm", "dry_run", "sanitize"]+ mcp-lifecycle-management: ["startup", "shutdown", "healthz"]+ mcp-multi-tenant: ["tenant", "isolation"] dynamic: true*** End Patch

This document summarizes which features are present, partially present, or missing after our patches, and references key evidence.

API keys act as identity but all clients share the same tool pool and data context (no tenant-specific segregation). | *Legend:* **Present** – feature implemented and in use; **Partial** – feature partially implemented or planned; **Missing** – not implemented (gap). ## 2. Implementation Details by Category **Protocol Surface & Tool Registry:** The MCP server exposes a RESTful API (via FastAPI in ITA) and a JSON-RPC interface for tool calls. We added an in-process JSON-RPC bridge (`server.py`) with support for listing available tools and invoking them. The `MCPToolRegistry` class holds tool definitions (name, description, endpoint) and is used to serve `listTools` results and route `callTool` requests to the correct backend action. For example, the registry registers tools like "kb_search" pointing to the ITA `/kb/search` endpoint, enabling dynamic discovery of capabilities. This aligns with the Model Context Protocol pattern of providing a tool catalog:contentReference[oaicite:23]{index=23}. **Schema Validation:** All endpoints use Pydantic models for input/output (e.g., `KnowledgeSearchRequest` in ITA), and the OpenAPI spec is up-to-date:contentReference[oaicite:24]{index=24}:contentReference[oaicite:25]{index=25}. This ensures that incoming requests are validated against a schema automatically. The audit’s `mcp-schema-validation` detector finds widespread `BaseModel` usage and the presence of `openapi.yaml` as evidence of robust schema enforcement. **Auth & AuthZ (Authentication and Authorization) & Safeguards:** The ITA requires each request to include a valid API key (`X-API-Key`) and a unique request ID (`X-Request-Id`):contentReference[oaicite:26]{index=26}. We encapsulated this in `MCPAuthenticator`, which uses the existing API key store and verification logic:contentReference[oaicite:27]{index=27}. Upon each request, the middleware uses this authenticator to reject unauthorized calls with a consistent error structure (returning an `Unauthorized` error). Authorization is currently all-or-nothing: any valid API key can invoke any tool (there are no role-based access controls yet), enforced by `MCPAuthorizer` always returning True. Additional safeguards are present: sensitive actions like Git PR creation require a confirmation flag and default to dry-run:contentReference[oaicite:28]{index=28}, preventing accidental changes. These patterns (confirm/dry_run) are explicitly documented and implemented in code, contributing to a **Present** status for security safeguards. Input validation (via Pydantic) also acts as a safeguard by rejecting malformed data. **Observability & Rate Limiting:** The system logs each request’s trace ID and propagates it in responses:contentReference[oaicite:29]{index=29}, which helps in tracing and debugging across components. We have a structured logging facility (JSON logs aligned with OpenTelemetry conventions) in the codebase, though applying it uniformly to MCP actions is a next step (currently, logging is minimal in MCP bridge). For observability, a `/metrics` endpoint is not yet exposed in ITA (the infrastructure exists, but ITA doesn’t serve it), so metrics are partial. We introduced `MCPRateLimiter` as a token-bucket limiter to throttle requests per principal. It uses an in-memory bucket that refills at a fixed rate and enforces a limit (e.g., 5 requests/sec burst 20 in FastAPI middleware). In the JSON-RPC server, a similar limiter prevents tool overuse. This is a basic implementation (memory-only, single-instance); in a distributed setting, we’d move to a shared store (Redis, etc.). The presence of this limiter moves rate limiting from Missing to Partial: the functionality exists and is detected by the audit (via `RateLimiter` and `RateLimitExceeded` usage), but could be expanded (e.g., configurable quotas, distributed enforcement). **Error Handling & Versioning:** We implemented a unified error model with `MCPError` and subclasses for common error scenarios (e.g., `ToolNotFound`, `ValidationError`, `RateLimitExceeded`, `Unauthorized`):contentReference[oaicite:30]{index=30}:contentReference[oaicite:31]{index=31}. Each carries a machine-readable `code` and an HTTP status. The FastAPI app now catches these exceptions and returns a JSON with `{"code": <CODE>, "message": <MESSAGE>}` consistently, and the JSON-RPC bridge does the equivalent in the RPC error object. This follows best practices for API error responses (having a stable error code and descriptive message):contentReference[oaicite:32]{index=32}. The audit’s `mcp-error-handling` capability is now marked Present because we have a structured approach spanning both HTTP and RPC surfaces. For versioning, we define `MCP_VERSIONS = ["1.0"]` and a helper `negotiate_version()` that selects a common version given a client’s list. This isn’t heavily used yet (since both client and server assume 1.0), but it lays the groundwork for future multi-version support. The bridge includes a placeholder handling for a `negotiateVersion` method. Thus, versioning is Partial: the concept is recognized, but only one version is truly supported at the moment. **Lifecycle & Configuration:** There are no custom lifecycle controls (like graceful shutdown or dynamic reloading of tools) implemented – the server relies on FastAPI’s default behavior and OS signals. A health check endpoint (`/healthz`) exists to signal basic readiness (returns 200 OK if the app is running):contentReference[oaicite:33]{index=33}. However, no further lifecycle management (hot reload, etc.) is present, so this capability remains Missing. On configuration, we have multiple configuration sources: environment variables (for example, ITA_URL and ITA_API_KEY for the bridge) and files (`mcp.json`). We added an `mcp/config.py` module (and the audit detector looks for it and the JSON) to consolidate this, but currently the usage is straightforward (loading env vars directly where needed). In the future, a unified `MCPConfig` could parse `mcp.json` and provide typed config to both ITA and the bridge. As it stands, the config is partially centralized (the file exists, and code loads values from it), hence Partial status. **Multi-tenancy:** The system is single-tenant: all requests run under the same context except for API key differentiation. There is no logic to partition data or tools by tenant or user beyond authentication. For instance, if this were offered as a service, all clients would see the same tools and share rate limits globally. Addressing multi-tenancy would require significant new code (scoping data by tenant, per-tenant config, etc.). The audit correctly marks this as Missing — it’s acknowledged as a gap with no current implementation. ## 3. MCP Validation Checklist To verify that MCP capabilities are properly detected and integrated, use the following steps: | Step | Command or Check | Expected Outcome ||------|-------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|| 1. | Run `python scripts/space_traversal/audit_runner.py run` | Audit pipeline S1–S7 completes without errors (including new detectors). || 2. | Open `audit_artifacts/capabilities_raw.json` | Contains entries for all `mcp-*` capabilities (at least 11 new IDs). || 3. | Open `audit_artifacts/capabilities_scored.json` | Each `mcp-*` capability has a score and component breakdown (most will initially be low or partial). || 4. | Check `audit_artifacts/gaps.json` | Lists low-maturity MCP capabilities (score < 0.70) as current gaps to address. || 5. | Open the latest `reports/capability_matrix_*.md` | MCP capabilities appear in the table, with their scores and found/missing pattern counts. || 6. | Run `python scripts/space_traversal/audit_runner.py explain mcp-protocol-surface` | Shows detailed scoring for that capability (e.g., which patterns were found, weight normalization). || 7. | (Regression check) Use `audit_runner.py diff --old <prev_scores.json> --new audit_artifacts/capabilities_scored.json` | The diff should show only additions of `mcp-*` capabilities (no significant score drops for existing entries). | Following this checklist confirms that the new MCP detectors are active (Step 2: all IDs present) and that our integrations improved the audit scores for MCP areas. For example, after these patches, capabilities like **mcp-tooling-registry** and **mcp-error-handling** should no longer appear as “Missing” gaps but show Partial/Present with higher scores, reflecting our implemented features.
